new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (23-page excerpt of the archive.org scan of Lynch, Ross & Crowley 2002, The Oceanic Languages; excerpt p. 2 = printed p. 388). extracted text of that PDF gives, at lines 60-62: '1.3 Stress / Kaulong stress generally falls on the final syllable of a verb and on the penultimate / syllable of a noun.' -- identical to the reported quote (line-wrap only). The same sentence appears in lines 106-108 and in the djvu text (lines 88-90). I read the whole phonology section (1.1-1.5, printed pp. 387-389): the only other stress-related remark is 1.1 'The front vowels /i/ and /e/ are [I] and [E] in closed unstressed syllables but [i] and [e] elsewhere'; 1.2 is phonotactics, 1.4 reduplication…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is category-conditioned: verbs are generally stressed on the final syllable, nouns on the penultimate syllable. Stated as a tendency ('generally'); no rule given for other word classes, monosyllables aside.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the hedge 'generally' is the only qualification. Section 1.1 adds that /i/ and /e/ are [I] and [E] 'in closed unstressed syllables', implying stress is phonetically real, but gives no further placement detail.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in the phonology section of a grammar sketch; data from Au village (northern dialect). No discussion of phrase stress, clitics (e.g. the delimiter men) or affixed/reduplicated forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 states the sketch data were collected at Au village, in the northern dialect area of Kaulong (western division); Glottolog kaul1240 language-level, no sub-dialect glottocode assigned. The sketch is 'adapted by Malcolm Ross' from Craig Throop's unpublished mss (1989 OPD, 1992 Grammar Essentials) plus Ross's own fieldnotes.
